### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“There is no easy way from the earth to the stars.”

Latin

“Non est ad astra mollis e terris via.”

Word for word: “there is no soft road from the earth to the stars.” The adjective is mollis — soft, yielding, easy to tread — and most English versions render it “easy,” which keeps the sense but loses the tactile contrast with the hard road.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “There is no easy way from the earth to the stars.”
-   “To the stars through difficulties.”
-   “Per aspera ad astra.”

### Attribution notes

The line is from Seneca's tragedy Hercules Furens, at verse 437 — a play, not the Letters to Lucilius where most circulating Seneca quotations originate, and the two are constantly confused. It is also routinely merged with “per aspera ad astra,” a separate Latin motto that is not in Seneca and whose wording is later. The play's line is spoken inside the drama and carries the dramatic situation with it; the film-poster version has shed all of that.

#### About Seneca

Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE–65 CE) was a Cordoban-born Stoic, tragic playwright, and adviser—later forced suicide victim—under Nero.

### Interpretation

Seneca is using a physical image to rule out a shortcut. The stars are not reached by effortlessness but by a path that does not admit of ease, and the claim is that excellence in anything difficult has the same structure. In Stoic terms the obstacle is not external circumstance but the cultivation of judgment, which cannot be acquired by a single decision. The line is often quoted as encouragement; in context it is closer to a warning about the shape of the work.

#### Why it matters

It is a useful corrective to methods built on removing friction. What you actually want is usually on the far side of a difficulty you cannot design away, so the practical question is which friction is worth keeping.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “There is no easy way from the earth…”?

“There is no easy way from the earth…” comes from Hercules Furens, 437, attributed to Seneca.

#### What does Seneca mean by virtue?

Virtue ethics asks not only which acts are right, but what kind of person one becomes. Courage, justice, temperance, and wisdom are classic Western lists; Confucian ren and yi offer related but distinct vocabularies. This passage enters that discussion through virtue.

#### Is the wording of this Seneca quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “There is no easy way from the earth to the stars.” Forms in circulation that differ: There is no easy way from the earth to the stars. / To the stars through difficulties. / Per aspera ad astra. The Latin reads “Non est ad astra mollis e terris via.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

The line is from Seneca's tragedy Hercules Furens, at verse 437 — a play, not the Letters to Lucilius where most circulating Seneca quotations originate, and the two are constantly confused. It is also routinely merged with “per aspera ad astra,” a separate Latin motto that is not in Seneca and whose wording is later. The play's line is spoken inside the drama and carries the dramatic situation with it; the film-poster version has shed all of that.
